Affiliate vs Partner vs Referral Programs: The Difference

Revenue

In short: Affiliate programs pay professional publishers a commission per defined event, at scale. Partner programs are fewer, larger deals negotiated company to company. Referral schemes give existing customers small rewards for bringing people they know. Which one a company needs depends on who could plausibly send it a customer.

Key points

  • Affiliate is a strict performance channel: the company pays only when the defined event occurs.
  • Partner programs are run by people, and one platform partnership can outweigh an entire affiliate program.
  • Referral works when people already talk about the product and the reward prompts the conversation without corrupting it.
  • Do not run a partner program on affiliate software or an affiliate program with referral-sized rewards.
  • Affiliate and partner programs are distribution assets a company can own outright, especially in restricted categories.

Three different arrangements pay other people to bring a company customers. They share vocabulary, they are often run from the same software, and confusing them costs companies real money in the wrong terms offered to the wrong partners.

Affiliate programs

An affiliate program pays independent publishers a commission for customers they send. The publishers are professionals: comparison sites, review sites, content creators, newsletters, deal and coupon sites, sub-networks that aggregate smaller publishers. They choose products to promote based on the commission, the conversion rate, and the fit with their audience, and they do it at scale, across many programs at once.

The company sets terms: what event is paid for, how much, for how long after the click, what is prohibited. The program lives on an affiliate network, which recruits publishers, tracks clicks and conversions, and handles payments for a fee, or on a direct platform the company runs itself.

Affiliate is a performance channel in the strict sense: the company pays only when the defined event occurs. It scales with the number and quality of publishers recruited, and it is available to most categories the ad platforms restrict, because publishers decide what to carry.

Partner programs

A partner program is a relationship between companies rather than with individual publishers. Integration partners, resellers, agencies, platforms, and complementary products agree to distribute, recommend, or embed the company's product in exchange for revenue share, referral fees, co-marketing, or reciprocal distribution.

Partner deals are fewer, larger, slower, and negotiated individually. A single partnership with a platform that already has the customer relationship can outweigh an entire affiliate program. Partner programs are run by people, not software; the tracking and payment tools matter less than the relationship and the terms.

Referral schemes

A referral scheme pays existing customers, or sometimes employees, for bringing in people they know. The reward is usually small, account credit, a discount, a bonus, and the volume per referrer is low because each person knows a limited number of relevant others.

Referral works when the product is something people talk about anyway and the reward is enough to prompt the conversation without being enough to corrupt it. It is a product feature more than a marketing channel, and it is usually run from inside the product.

Which one a company needs

Ask who could plausibly send you a customer.

If the answer is professional publishers who already reach your buyer, comparison sites, creators, newsletters, you need an affiliate program, with terms designed to exclude the coupon leak.

If the answer is other companies whose customers are your customers, platforms, integrations, service providers, you need a partner program, and probably a person to run it.

If the answer is your own customers, you need a referral scheme, built into the product.

Most companies past a certain size need all three, run differently, and should not try to run a partner program on affiliate software or an affiliate program with referral-sized rewards.

Why they should be built and owned

Affiliate and partner programs are among the few distribution channels a company can own outright. The terms, the partner base, the reporting history, and the relationships are assets that keep working when any single ad platform changes its mind. For a company in a restricted category, they are usually the first thing worth building properly, and the last thing worth outsourcing to a network's default settings.

lowob takeaway: Affiliate pays professional publishers per event at scale; partner programs are negotiated company-to-company; referral rewards existing customers. Match the terms to the sender, and treat the first two as assets you own.

Common questions

What is the difference between an affiliate program and a referral program?

An affiliate program pays independent professional publishers, such as comparison sites, creators and newsletters, a commission for customers they send. A referral scheme pays existing customers, or sometimes employees, a small reward such as credit or a discount for bringing in people they know.

What is a partner program?

A partner program is a relationship between companies, such as integration partners, resellers, agencies and platforms, that distribute or recommend a product in exchange for revenue share, referral fees, co-marketing or reciprocal distribution. Deals are fewer, larger, slower and negotiated individually.

How do I decide whether I need an affiliate, partner or referral program?

Ask who could plausibly send you a customer. Professional publishers point to affiliate, other companies whose customers are yours point to a partner program, and your own customers point to a referral scheme built into the product.

Do companies need more than one type of program?

Most companies past a certain size need all three, run differently. Each needs terms matched to the sender.
